notes: Large six-claim judicial review of sexual orientation employment regulations; Richards J's conclusions on each impugned regulation are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Trade unions' challenge to sexual orientation employment equality exceptions
key_facts: Six trade union claimants, including Amicus and the NUT, sought to annul exceptions in the Employment Equality (Sexual Orientation) Regulations 2003 made under the European Communities Act 1972.
The challenged provisions were occupational requirement exceptions in regulations 7 and 20(3), especially for organised religion, and a marital status benefits exception in regulation 25.
Evangelical Christian organisations intervened in support of the Secretary of State, arguing the exceptions balanced religious freedom with anti-discrimination rights.
The unions argued the exceptions were incompatible with Directive 2000/78/EC and with articles 8 and 14 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claims seeking annulment of specified provisions of secondary legislation implementing an EU equality directive.
enrichment.outcome: All claims dismissed; the impugned regulations were held compatible with the Directive and Convention rights.
enrichment.ratio: The occupational requirement exceptions in regulations 7 and 20(3) were a lawful and proportionate implementation of Directive 2000/78/EC, including for employment by organised religions; regulation 25 fell within the Directive's limitation on marital status benefits and was not unlawfully discriminatory; the Regulations conferred rights rather than interfering with Convention rights, so the article 14 challenge failed.
legal_issues: Whether regulations 7(2) and 7(3) exceeded the power under section 2(2) of the European Communities Act 1972
Whether regulation 20(3) breached the Directive or the principle of legal certainty
Whether regulation 25 unlawfully permitted discrimination by reference to marital status
Whether the NUT could show a lowering of pre-existing national protection
Whether the impugned provisions breached articles 8 and 14 ECHR
linked_authorities: Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] EWCA Civ 1533
R v Lord Chancellor, ex parte Witham [1998] QB 575

confidence.notes: Outcome and regulation-by-regulation analysis are clear. Some linked ECJ and comparative authorities are cited illustratively rather than as core ratio.

notes: Short asylum credibility appeal; adjudicator's Egypt/Egyptian errors and thin reasoning are central and clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Ahmadi asylum appeal after adjudicator's credibility errors
key_facts: A Pakistani Ahmadi appellant claimed asylum on grounds of religious persecution but his appeal was dismissed by an adjudicator who doubted his credibility.
The adjudicator's determination wrongly referred to Egypt, Egyptian warrants, and evidence given in Egyptian, despite the appellant being from Pakistan.
The IAT refused leave, criticising the appellant's travel account including a reference to the 'Cameroon islands'.
Jackson J refused permission for judicial review, but the Court of Appeal granted permission and heard the substantive appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted against refusal of permission to seek judicial review of an IAT leave refusal following dismissal of an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal; respondent ordered to pay the legally aided appellant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where an asylum decision turns centrally on an adjudicator's credibility findings, strange and unexplained errors of fact together with thin reasoning can render the determination unsatisfactory and require the case to be reconsidered, even if isolated mistakes do not appear in the decisive paragraph.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator gave adequate reasons for disbelieving the appellant's account
Whether mistaken references to Egypt and the Egyptian language vitiated the determination
Whether the IAT's reasoning on the appellant's travel route was justified
Whether ex parte Haile governed cases involving more extreme adjudicator errors
linked_authorities: R v Immigration Appeal Tribunal ex parte Haile [2001] EWCA Civ 663

notes: Interlocutory judgment after post-hearing DFG developments; Charles J declined to decide construction points and relief was not finally settled in the text.

enrichment.short_title: MS patient's home adaptations: CSDPA duty versus DFG route

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970
Health and Social Services Adjudications Act 1983
Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: A 58-year-old man with multiple sclerosis living in his estranged wife's owned home needed disability adaptations assessed under community care legislation.
A disabilities facilities grant application had not succeeded because the wife would not disclose her means or contribute to costs.
Both parties initially assumed Mrs F's means barred a DFG and argued whether Essex County Council had a section 2 CSDPA 1970 duty to fund the works.
After the hearing Chelmsford Borough Council indicated a DFG might be available with Mrs F's means disregarded if she applied, as the couple were not members of the same household.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge to a local authority decision on funding home adaptations, heard on a provisional basis pending further DFG information.
enrichment.outcome: Held that the section 2 CSDPA 1970 duty had not arisen because a DFG was likely available; the court did not finally decide the construction and reasonableness issues argued at the hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where necessary adaptations can reasonably be funded through the usual DFG route once household and means rules are properly applied, a local authority is not required at that stage to treat it as necessary for it to fund the works under section 2 CSDPA 1970; the parties' shared misunderstanding about DFG availability affected the issues properly before the court.
legal_issues: Whether section 2 CSDPA 1970 imposed a duty to fund adaptations in the claimant's home
Whether means testing under section 17 HASSA 1983 affected the existence of the section 2 duty
Whether Mrs F's means could be taken into account for a DFG where she and the claimant were not the same household
Whether costs could be recovered from Mrs F under section 17 if adaptations were provided under section 2

notes: Consent order construction on net proceeds after mortgage discharge by endowment policies; appellate reasoning is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Net proceeds of sale under consent order after mortgage discharge
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Bishop agreed a 1998 consent order dividing net proceeds of sale of the matrimonial home, with specified splits up to and above £159,000.
The husband died in 1999 before sale; endowment policies discharged the mortgage through internal Lloyds Bank movements.
The house sold in 2002 for £275,000, far above the figure contemplated in 1998.
The husband's estate argued the mortgage deduction should be the notional amount outstanding at the consent order date, not nil after policy payout.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal with permission granted on a point of construction of a consent order, following conflicting county court decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; district judge's order reinstated; respondent to pay the appellant's costs of the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: In calculating 'net proceeds of sale' under a consent order, the mortgage deduction is the amount outstanding at the time of sale, not a fictional historic balance; where endowment policies discharged the mortgage before sale, that deduction falls away consistently with how estate agents' and conveyancing costs are treated.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'net proceeds of sale' in the consent order recitals
Whether the mortgage deduction should be taken at the consent order date or at completion
Whether implementation of the order amounted to variation rather than construction
Whether permission to appeal should be granted under section 55 of the Access to Justice Act 1999
linked_authorities: Thompson v Thompson [1955] 2 All ER 243

notes: Leading-style analysis of Lloyd's amenability to judicial review and HRA section 6 in regulatory buy-out context.

enrichment.short_title: Whether Lloyd's minority buy-out decisions are amenable to judicial review
key_facts: Dr Julian West challenged Business Conduct Committee approvals of four minority buy-outs of his Lloyd's syndicate participations under the Major Syndicate Transactions Byelaw.
Keith J refused permission for judicial review on the basis Lloyd's was not a public authority exercising public functions.
The Court of Appeal reserved and tried first whether Lloyd's was amenable to judicial review, including under section 6 HRA.
Lloyd's members participate voluntarily under contractual membership obligations, while prudential regulation is now exercised by the FSA under FSMA.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reserved preliminary issue on amenability to judicial review and public authority status under the Human Rights Act, following grant of permission to apply for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that Lloyd's is not amenable to judicial review, whether under section 6 HRA or otherwise, in relation to the impugned regulatory buy-out functions; Dr West would need to begin fresh private law proceedings if so advised.
enrichment.ratio: Lloyd's exercise of powers under the MST Byelaw over members' syndicate participations is a private contractual regulatory function, not a governmental or public function; the FSA performs the governmental regulatory role under FSMA, so Lloyd's is not a public authority within section 6 HRA for these decisions.
legal_issues: Whether Lloyd's Council and committee decisions on minority buy-outs are amenable to judicial review
Whether Lloyd's is a public authority under section 6(1) and (3)(b) HRA
Whether statutory incorporation by private Act and market regulation create a public law element
Whether ex parte Datafin supports treating Lloyd's buy-out decisions as public functions

R v Panel on Take-overs and Mergers, ex p Datafin plc [1987] QB 815
Poplar Housing Association Ltd v Donoghue [2001] EWCA Civ 595

Aston Cantlow PCC v Wallbank [2003] UKHL 37

notes: Short administrators' directions application; Neuberger J precedent applied clearly to Schedule B1 wording.

enrichment.short_title: Administrators' power to sell assets before creditor approval of proposals
key_facts: Administrators of Transbus International Ltd sought directions on whether they could sell company assets before creditors approved their proposals.
Under the pre-Enterprise Act regime Neuberger J in Re T&D Industries had held administrators could sell without prior court direction.
Schedule B1 to the Insolvency Act 1986, introduced by the Enterprise Act 2002, uses slightly different wording in paragraph 68.
The court was asked whether paragraph 68(1) made court directions mandatory before any pre-proposal disposals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrators' application for directions under paragraph 63 of Schedule B1 to the Insolvency Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Administrators held to have power to sell assets before creditor approval of proposals without obtaining court directions, consistent with Re T&D Industries.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 68(2) of Schedule B1 requires compliance with court directions only if the court gives them; it does not require administrators to obtain directions before acting, and the Enterprise Act policy of reducing court involvement supports the same approach as under the former section 17 Insolvency Act 1986.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 68(1) Schedule B1 prevents disposals before proposals are approved
Whether paragraph 68(2) makes court directions a precondition to administrators acting
Whether Re T&D Industries remains good law after the Enterprise Act 2002 amendments
linked_authorities: Re T&D Industries plc [2000] 1 WLR 646

notes: Long first-instance judgment on HIV-positive asylum seeker section 21 duty; quashing order and reassessment direction are clear.

enrichment.short_title: HIV-positive asylum seeker's section 21 accommodation duty
key_facts: M, a Zimbabwean asylum seeker with HIV/AIDS, was accommodated by Slough Borough Council while his asylum claim remained undetermined.
He could not work, relied on charitable support for food, and needed refrigerated medication and stable accommodation to avoid deterioration.
Slough assessed that he was not in need of care and attention under section 21 NAA 1948 and sought to pass responsibility to NASS.
Section 21(1A) excludes asylum seekers whose need for care and attention arises solely from destitution or its physical effects.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local authority needs assessment refusing continuing section 21 accommodation for a destitute asylum seeker with HIV/AIDS.
enrichment.outcome: Assessment quashed; Slough required to reassess in light of the judgment; permission to appeal granted; costs ordered in the claimant's favour.
enrichment.ratio: A chronically ill asylum seeker may be in need of care and attention for section 21 purposes not solely because of destitution; where loss of accommodation would disproportionately harm an HIV-positive person, or ongoing medical care itself constitutes a need for care and attention, the section 21(1A) exclusion does not transfer responsibility to NASS.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'care and attention' under section 21(1)(a) NAA 1948
Whether destitution alone can create a section 21 duty for asylum seekers
Application of section 21(1A) and the section 95 destitution test
Allocation of support between local authorities and NASS after Westminster v NASS and Mani

notes: Detailed trust deed construction on short leasehold proviso and estoppel; declaration for claimants is explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Debenture trust deed withdrawal of short leasehold security
key_facts: Queen's Moat Houses and Norfolk sought to withdraw the Royal Court Hotel lease from debenture stock security under a 1983 trust deed.
The trust deed's 'value' definition included a proviso attributing nil value to short leaseholds expiring within 45 years after stock maturity.
The Sloane Square lease was a short leasehold but had been charged in 1994 to improve fixed security during a restructuring.
Security cover was only marginally above the 150% minimum and the claimants were in financial distress.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for declaration on construction of trust deed clauses governing substitution and withdrawal of specifically mortgaged property.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants entitled to withdraw the Sloane Property on payment of transaction expenses; estoppel by convention claim rejected.
enrichment.ratio: The short leasehold proviso in the definition of 'value' applies to withdrawals under clause 11 of the trust deed; a contractual right to require release of charged property does not convert a fixed charge into a floating charge, and estoppel by convention requires convincing proof equivalent to rectification.
legal_issues: Whether the short leasehold proviso applies to clause 11 substitution and withdrawal
Whether a unilateral withdrawal right recharacterises a fixed charge as floating
Whether estoppel by convention prevented nil-value withdrawal
Commercial purpose of protecting stockholders from diminution of security

BCCI v Ali [2002] 1 AC 251
Smith v Bridgend County Borough Council [2002] 1 BCLC 89
T&N Ltd v Royal & Sun Alliance [2004] 2 LLR 106

notes: Magistrates' courts service rule challenge with declaration and guidance quashed; statutory analysis is direct.

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates cannot require personal service after lawful postal service
key_facts: Durham County Council prosecuted parking fine defaulters by summons served by post to last known addresses under Rule 99(1)(c).
North Durham Justices adjourned cases for personal service because summonses lacked dates of birth and other 'essential information' under court guidance.
Personal service was costly and often impracticable, threatening effective parking enforcement across several local authority areas.
All underlying prosecutions had by the hearing been withdrawn or concluded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with appeal by way of case stated challenging justices' policy requiring personal service despite postal service under Rule 99.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that justices have no power to order personal service where defendants were lawfully served under Rule 99(1); costs of judicial review awarded to the council subject to possible magistrates' representations.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 99 gives prosecutors a choice among prescribed methods of service and 'may' does not confer discretion on justices to reject valid postal service; once service under Rule 99(1) is proved, section 11 Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 permits trial in absence without ordering personal service for missing non-statutory details.
legal_issues: Whether justices had discretion under Rule 99 to require personal service
Whether incomplete defendant identification details invalidated postal service
Whether judicial review or case stated was the appropriate remedy at an interlocutory stage
Lawfulness of justices' chief executive guidance on essential defendant information
linked_authorities: Streames v Copping [1985] 2 All ER 122
Atkinson v United States Government [1969] 3 All ER 1317

notes: Commercial Court forum conveniens and service-out application; Morison J's detailed Spiliada analysis supports dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Retrocession dispute: service out and forum conveniens
key_facts: Munich Re sought declarations and recovery of payments from Canadian retrocedent Commonwealth under a London-market retrocession of a US excess property programme.
Moore-Bick J granted permission to serve out in Canada under CPR 6.20 on the basis the contract was made in England and governed by English law.
Commonwealth commenced parallel proceedings in California against Munich Re and broker THB, arguing a follow-the-settlements obligation and arbitration.
The Mexico fire claim turned on construction of the retrocession slip, underlying master policy terms, and whether a local policy was required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside an order granting permission to serve the claim form out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; England held the more appropriate forum; service of suit clause held to be Canada rather than USA.
enrichment.ratio: Where a London-market retrocession contract is governed by English law and its construction is the centre of gravity of the dispute, England is the appropriate forum despite parallel contingent broker proceedings abroad; a contingent claim against a producing broker should not displace trial of the principal reinsurance dispute, and the service of suit clause referred to Canada.
legal_issues: Whether Munich Re established a good arguable case within CPR 6.20
Whether England was clearly and distinctly the most appropriate forum under Spiliada
Whether parallel California proceedings against THB required a single forum trial
Proper construction of the service of suit clause and governing law of the retrocession contract
linked_authorities: Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460
Insurance Corporation of Ireland v Strombus [1985] 2 Lloyd's Rep 138
Trade Indemnity v Njord [1995] LRLR 367
Aneco v J & H [1998] 1 Lloyd's Rep 565
